The input is the SPEC, not a medium to preserve. Output a PHOTOGRAPH of real cloth, never a colored-in drawing.
READ THE INPUT, WHATEVER THE MEDIUM (sketch, illustration, digital flat, croquis, spec sheet, photo of a sketch, or photo of a real garment):
- Any drawing is the spec to build from. Discard the paper, page edges, notebook lines, desk, hands, page tilt, watermarks, annotations, arrows, and callout leader lines — a callout line touching the garment edge is not a seam or strap.
- A croquis figure under the garment is NOT part of the design. Its bare arms, hands, shoulders, neck, and legs are SKIN, never fabric. NEVER convert a bare arm into a sleeve. Any limb drawn in skin tone, or drawn outside the garment's colored fill, is the body — omit it entirely.
- A photo of a real garment: keep its exact design and fabric, re-shot in the presentation below (swatch and notes still override fabric and color).
- The same garment from several angles is ONE garment: merge every angle into one understanding and photograph it once, front facing, unless the notes ask otherwise.
- A SET of separate pieces meant to be worn together: render ALL pieces as one worn look in ghost form, each distinct — never fuse, drop, or add a piece.
- A tight detail crop (cuff, collar, pocket): shoot that detail as a macro fabric-and-construction close-up, don't invent the rest of the garment.
MEDIUM — DRAWING IN, PHOTOGRAPH OUT. This matters most. Completely transform the medium: kill every trace of drawing — white paper, outline strokes, flat cel-shaded fills, hatching, marker streaks, vector flatness. Do not tint, trace, or clean up the drawing; re-photograph from scratch. Build the garment from real cloth: true textile with thread-level detail, visible grain, stitch definition, physical drape and gravity, on a high-end camera under soft even studio softbox light with gentle real shadows and true highlights. If any pencil line, paper white, or illustration flatness survives, the render has FAILED.
FABRIC & CONSTRUCTION REALISM — render like a garment technician:
- Commit to ONE plausible fabric the design implies (notes/swatch override) and keep its true hand everywhere: crisp poplin, dry wool suiting, fluid crepe, airy chiffon, dense ponte, soft jersey — with the weave or knit structure visible up close and light behaving like that exact textile.
- Construction reads as sewn, not painted: seams and hems at true stitch scale with the slight pucker of real sewing; collars roll on a collar stand, never pressed flat; buttons, buttonholes, zippers, and hardware with real thread, teeth, and metal weight.
- Cloth obeys gravity: tension folds, soft hem breaks, plumb grainline, natural micro-wrinkles — perfect mathematical smoothness is a failure.
- Never: plastic, waxy, or airbrushed surfaces; repeating CGI ripple-folds; melted or wandering seams; sketch outlines re-rendered as piping or embroidery; HDR glow or bokeh.
- This governs HOW drawn details render; it never adds seams, stitching, trims, closures, or fabrics the design doesn't show.
PRESERVE THE DESIGN EXACTLY — reproduce, don't redesign or normalize: silhouette and proportions (an oversized, cropped, or exaggerated cut stays exactly that); seam, dart, panel, and yoke placement; neckline shape and depth; collar/lapel type; closure type, position, and count (match countable buttons/snaps); sleeve presence, style, length; cuff, hem shape and length; vents, slits, pleats, gathers, waistband, drawcord, pockets, topstitching, hardware. Read ambiguous lines the most literal way. Structure, type, and proportion may not be changed; only very fine placement may be approximated. Add nothing the design doesn't show — no extra layers, accessories, or props.
SLEEVES AND ARMHOLES — decide from the GARMENT'S OWN fabric outline, NEVER from the figure's arms:
- The garment has a sleeve ONLY where its own fabric visibly covers the arm. Render each real sleeve at its exact drawn length and cut.
- If the shoulders and arms are bare skin (the arms belong to the croquis, not the dress), the garment is SLEEVELESS. Render clean, finished armhole openings and any straps exactly as drawn, with NO sleeve, NO fabric tube, NO sheer or transparent sleeve, and NO arm. Do not fill the space where the figure's arms were.
- Shoulder details (gathered caps, ruching, clips, straps, epaulettes) are NOT sleeves — reproduce them at their real small size, never grown into a sleeve.
PRESENTATION — GHOST FORM / INVISIBLE MANNEQUIN:
CAMERA: straight-on at eye level, front squared and parallel to camera — no tilt, no three-quarter rotation, no top-down. Ignore the drawn figure's pose and stance entirely (hand on hip, weight shift, turned hips, crossed legs); always rebuild the garment squared and symmetric to the camera. Soft even studio light.
BACKGROUND: seamless pure-white studio sweep, evenly lit edge to edge, garment alone with a soft natural grounding shadow.
FORM: filled to natural worn 3D volume — shoulders level, side seams plumb, center-front vertical, hem level. IF the garment has sleeves, they carry implied arm volume and hang DOWNWARD at the sides with a slight, equal, SYMMETRIC bend, cuffs pointing down — never straight out, twisted, or gaping at the camera. IF the garment is SLEEVELESS, show open finished armholes and bare straps with empty space where an arm would be — no sleeve, no arm, no filled fabric.
NO BODY, EVER: no person or mannequin visible — no head, face, hair, neck, skin, arms, hands, legs, feet, torso, no human silhouette, no translucent/ghostly figure, no mesh form, no partial limbs. Worn by nothing.
OPENINGS/INTERIOR: any opening facing the camera (neckline, hood, open front, waist) reveals the real INTERIOR — inner panel, collar stand, facing or lining — rendered slightly darker in soft shadow, with readable fabric detail and color. NEVER a solid black hole, void, or empty cutout; the inside is real cloth in shadow.
FRAMING: centered, fully in view with even margins at any aspect ratio — add background around the garment for tall/wide outputs, never crop a cuff/hem/edge, no letterboxing.
FOR A SET: arrange the pieces as one worn look (correctly layered and overlapping), all in ghost form, centered and uncropped.

inputs.description: The garment to recolor. Can be shown on a model, as a flatlay, or in ghostform
inputs.name: Garment

prompts.prompt:
Input Roles: 
- BASE_IMAGE (Image 1): Owns the garment, its presentation, composition, shape, details, lighting, and all non-edited pixels


- GARMENT_MASK (Image 2): a cutout of Image 1. Only the pixels to recolor are visible; everything else is transparent and may render as black. It is a selection, not a reference photo of the garment.
- TARGET_COLOR: the color reference (what color to apply) 

Task: Recolor part of the garment in Image 1 to [TARGET_COLOR].


Image 2 is a selection map, not a photo to copy from. It was cut out of Image 1: the region to recolor appears with its original fabric pixels, and everything else is transparent (note: transparent may be rendered as black). Treat the fabric visible in Image 2 as a stencil that marks where to edit. Do not copy its current color, do not treat it as a color reference, and do not recolor anything that is black in Image 2.


Before editing, find the visible region of Image 2 on Image 1 and identify what it covers. It may be only part of a garment: a collar, one sleeve, a zipper, a panel. If so, only that part changes. The rest of that same garment keeps its original color even where the fabric is identical.


Rules:
- Change hue only. Keep the fabric texture, weave, folds, seams, shadows, highlights, and lighting exactly as they are in Image 1.
- Stop the new color exactly at the edge of the visible region. No bleed onto skin, background, hardware, adjacent clothing, or the un-selected part of the same garment.
- Every pixel that is transparent or black in Image 2 is copied from Image 1 unchanged: subject, pose, framing, resolution, other garments.


Output one photorealistic image, identical to Image 1 except the selected region, which is now [TARGET_COLOR].


[TARGET_COLOR]:

PRESENTATION LOCK
First determine the presentation of BASE_IMAGE:
- ON_MODEL: garment is worn by a person.
- FLATLAY: garment is laid flat on a surface.
- GHOST_FORM: garment is displayed without a visible person, such as an invisible
  mannequin, hangerless product view, or hollow garment form.


Preserve that presentation exactly. Never add, remove, invent, or alter a person,
mannequin, hanger, body, limbs, styling, surface, or background. The output must be
the same presentation and composition as BASE_IMAGE, not a try-on unless BASE_IMAGE
already is one.

EDIT BOUNDARY (Highest priority)
Use the masked area to define exactly what to recolor. Keep the garment's shape, fit, drape, and proportions pixel-identical to the source; recolor only the pixels within the mask boundary.

Render the recolored garment as if it were always this color on the same model in the same pose, lighting, and camera. Preserve all existing fabric texture, stitching detail, seams, zippers, hardware, and surface properties—only the hue and saturation change, not the material or construction.

The boundary where the recolored garment meets skin or adjacent garments must remain seamless, with no visible cut-line, halo, or composite edge. Respect the mask's soft edges exactly; feathering and anti-aliasing in the mask are preserved, not sharpened or re-feathered.

Where the mask has reduced opacity (grays), scale the recolor intensity proportionally so transition zones blend naturally into preserved areas.


The output is the source photograph with this single garment recolored, its shape, drape, folds, contact points with the body, face, hair, pose, skin, body shape, and every other garment or accessory not covered by the recolor mask pixel-identical to the source.
If the cutout covers only part of a garment (a collar, a sleeve, a zipper, a panel), recolor only that part. Never extend the recolor to the rest of that garment.
2. Hue:
Shift only the Hue toward the target; preserve the original per-pixel Saturation and Lightness relationships so highlights still blow toward white and shadows deepen naturally under the scene's existing lighting.
Reproduce the reference hue literally. Do not stylize, warm, cool, or "improve" the color.


3. Texture & realism:
Preserve fabric weave, thread sheen, wrinkles, folds, shadows, highlights, grain, and sharpness from Image 1. The result should look like fabric manufactured in this color, not painted over it.

Do NOT: flat fill, posterize, halo or glow at edges, plastic/CGI look, loss of texture, altered pose/framing/resolution, or any change to unmasked pixels.
Before finalizing, verify: (1) verify every pixel that is not visible in Image 2 is unchanged, (2) the recolored hue matches Image 3, (3) fabric texture and lighting are intact.
Output: a single photorealistic image, identical to Image 1 except the masked region recolored to [TARGET_COLOR].
[TARGET_COLOR]:

Recolor the garment in Image 1 to [TARGET_COLOR], using Image 2 as the exact mask defining the region to edit, and using Image 3 as the exact color reference to apply.


Rules:
- Sample the exact target color from Image 3 and apply it ONLY within the white area of the mask (Image 2). Leave all black-masked regions of Image 1 completely unchanged.
- Preserve the original fabric texture, weave, folds, shadows, highlights, and lighting. Only the hue should change to match Image 3; keep luminance and material detail intact.
- Maintain edges precisely along the mask boundary with no color bleed onto skin, background, buttons, or adjacent clothing.
- Keep the subject, pose, framing, resolution, and all unmasked details identical to Image 1.


Output a single photorealistic image of the same try-on with the masked region naturally recolored to the exact color shown in Image 3 ([TARGET_COLOR]).

prompts.prompt:
Create the execution specification for this one fabric swap.

BASE_IMAGE = @[garment-flatlay-or-ghostform] 
BASE_GARMENT_MASK = @[garment-mask] 
FABRIC = @[fabric] 

@[garment-flatlay-or-ghostform] is always the canvas and @[fabric] is always fabric evidence. Apply only the material shown in @[fabric] to the region(s) selected by @[garment-mask] Never reverse these roles.

CANVAS LOCK:
Preserve the BASE_IMAGE frame, dimensions, crop, viewpoint, model identity, pose, anatomy, facial features, hair, sunglasses, background, and studio lighting setup. Do not use the FABRIC image as a canvas.

TARGET GARMENT:
The selected garment is the cropped color-block motorcycle jacket on the model’s upper body. Replace only the jacket’s black fabric/colorway panels with the FABRIC material, including the visible black shoulder/chest inserts and any black jacket fabric areas identified by the mask. Keep the blue and white leather panels unchanged. Preserve the black printed FLORA FAUNA lettering on the white panels as existing surface graphics, not as fabric to replace.

SOURCE FABRIC:
Use the FABRIC reference only as material: a dark black-to-charcoal woven ripstop textile with a fine basketlike weave, subtle raised grid lines, faint diagonal reinforcement structure, low-to-moderate technical sheen, and visible thread texture.

PATTERN SCALE AND MAPPING:
Map the ripstop grid realistically onto the jacket’s black panels at garment scale. The grid should follow each jacket panel’s curvature, perspective, seams, folds, and tension, with alignment breaking naturally at cut-and-sewn panel boundaries. Continue the square grid repeat beyond the reference where needed without adding new motifs.

MATERIAL AND FINISH:
Render the replaced black jacket panels as structured black technical woven fabric rather than smooth leather. Keep the color deep black/charcoal, with restrained highlights from the studio lights, visible woven texture, and raised grid definition. Maintain the jacket’s existing fold shadows and panel shading, recalculated for the less glossy ripstop surface.

GARMENT LOCK:
Preserve the jacket’s exact cropped silhouette, volume, fit, seams, panel shapes, collar, sleeves, cuffs, hem, zipper placement, pocket zippers, snaps, stitching, and construction. Do not alter the jacket design, proportions, length, drape, or color-block layout.

LAYERING AND OCCLUSION:
Keep the crossbody bag and strap in front of the jacket exactly where they occlude it. Preserve all hardware, zippers, snaps, printed lettering, sunglasses, pants, gloves, bags, shoes, and accessories in their original positions. Do not apply the fabric to pants, gloves, bags, sunglasses, background, or any non-jacket black object.

LOCAL RECONSTRUCTION AND LIGHTING:
Blend the new fabric only across the selected black jacket panels and a narrow seam/contact band. Match the base photo’s white studio lighting, shadow softness, focus, grain, and white balance. Reconstruct any partially covered black jacket panel areas behind occluders only where visible and consistent with the existing jacket.

DO NOT TRANSFER:
Do not transfer the fabric reference’s folds, wrinkles, crop, lighting, shadows, blur, surface defects, or camera perspective. Do not transfer any objects or background from the fabric image. Do not invent logos, text, embroidery, or additional patterning beyond the visible ripstop weave and grid.

FABRIC ADJUSTMENTS:
Apply the adjustment so all black colorway fabric areas of the selected jacket are replaced with the new ripstop fabric. Leave non-black jacket colorways unchanged.

You are the Fabric Swap Director for a local fashion-photo edit. Your job is to inspect the visual inputs, resolve their roles, and write one concise execution specification for an image-editing model.
ROLE BINDING IS ABSOLUTE
- BASE_IMAGE may show a garments worn on a model or a garment alone (faltlay, ghost-form, hanger, or packshot); both are valid. the photo being edited. It owns the final output: dimensions, any person present (identity, anatomy, pose), camera, lighting environment, background, every object, and the garment's cut, construction, silhouette, and drape.
- BASE_GARMENT_MASK answers which garment receives the new fabric; the garment's own visible extent answers where the new fabric appears.
- Ignore minor mask spill onto skin, hair, hands, accessories, adjacent garments, people, and background.
- A partial mask may identify a garment that continues behind an occluder or beyond the selected area. Apply the new fabric to the entire visible garment; leave no leftover patches of the original fabric.
- Do not change the fabric of any other garment or object in the base image.
- FABRIC is the fabric reference. It may be a flat swatch, folded or draped yardage, a bolt, a close-up detail, or fabric shown on another object or garment. It is never the photo being edited, and nothing transfers from it except the fabric itself.
MASK INTERPRETATION AND RECOVERY
- Treat the mask as the authoritative selection of the edit target (s), not as a cutout and not as a stencil for the pattern. 
- Resolve each disconnected mask region independently:
- If a region covers most of a garment's visible extent, with gaps explained by occluders (hair, arms, bags, overlapping garments), the target is the ENTIRE garment: apply the new fabric to its full visible extent, including parts continuing beyond the mask or behind occluders, leaving no leftover patches of the original fabric.
- If a region deliberately covers only a construction-bounded portion of a garment (one sleeve, the collar, the bodice, a pocket), the target is exactly that portion: apply the new fabric only within it, ending the swap cleanly at the portion's natural seams and edges, and leave the rest of that garment's original fabric fully untouched. A portion-level mask is a design decision, not an error to correct.
- When the mask has multiple regions, every region receives its swap in the same single output; do not drop, merge, or expand any region, regardless of how far apart the regions are.
- Ignore minor mask spill onto skin, hair, hands, accessories, adjacent garments, people, and background — but never ignore a region's deliberate boundary at a seam.

TRANSFER FROM THE FABRIC
- fabric category and identity: weave or knit structure, fiber character, and construction as visibly supported
- color, dye effects, pattern, print, motif set, and repeat
- surface texture, yarn and weave scale, pile, nap, slub, and grain direction
- sheen, reflectance, transparency, and finish that are visibly supported by the fabric reference
- TEXTURE NAMING
Name the fabric in one line using precise textile terms, stacking: construction + surface + finish + scale + light response. Example: "3x1 indigo twill denim, slubbed warp, stonewashed matte finish, weave visible at close range, flat light absorption with pale highlights on fold ridges." Use 3-5 terms max, and only what the fabric reference visibly shows — never upgrade a plain fabric to a fancier construction.
PATTERN SCALE AND MAPPING
- Size the pattern realistically for the garment, using scale cues in the fabric reference (weave detail, thread size, recognizable objects) when present; otherwise use a scale typical for that fabric on that garment category.
- The pattern must follow the garment's real shape: wrap around the body, bend across folds and perspective, and break or realign at seams the way cut-and-sewn panels do.
- Do not lay the fabric image flat over the garment like a sticker or decal.
- Continue the pattern beyond what the reference shows using only the visible repeat and symmetry.
ADAPT FOR BASE_IMAGE
- scale and perspective
- the base photo's lighting: direction, color, softness, reflections, focus, grain, and white balance
- how the new fabric responds to that lighting: highlights, matte diffusion, translucency, and contact shadows true to the material
- the garment's existing folds and shadows, re-shaded to match the new fabric
NEVER TRANSFER FROM FABRIC
- any object, garment shape, body, hands, mannequin, hanger, table, surface, or background visible in the fabric reference
- the reference's own wrinkles, folds, crumple, drape, cut edges, selvage, fraying, tags, labels, rulers, color cards, watermarks, or text outside the printed pattern
- the fabric photo's lighting, shadows, highlights, color cast, crop, camera, or image defects; carry over the fabric's true color and texture, not the lighting it was photographed in
- garment design features such as collars, plackets, buttons, seams, or hems if the fabric reference happens to show a finished garment
GARMENT AND BASE PRESERVATION
- When a person is present, preserve their exact identity, anatomy, pose, proportions, face, hair, hands, and expression. exact identity, anatomy, pose, proportions, face, hair, hands, and expression. - Preserve the base frame, crop, aspect ratio, viewpoint, background, and all other garments and objects.
- Preserve the garment's exact cut, silhouette, proportions, length, volume, fit, drape, folds, tension, seams, panels, darts, pleats, pockets, collar, neckline, sleeves, cuffs, waist, and hem.
- Preserve closures, hardware, trims, and topstitching in their exact position and shape; settle them onto the new fabric without moving, redesigning, deleting, or duplicating them.
- Preserve base accessories and jewelry in their exact screen position and shape, and keep every base occluder such as hair, hands, arms, bags, and outer layers in front of the garment wherever it was in front of the old fabric.
- The editable regions is only the selected target's surface (the whole garment, or the masked portion). Treat everything outside it as locked. 

SILHOUETTE LOCK
The fabric changes; the garment does not. Do not let the new fabric's implied weight, stiffness, or stretch alter the garment's shape, drape, volume, length, or fit. Re-render the existing shape in the new fabric. If the new fabric is sheer or open-weave, render see-through areas conservatively, reconstructing only the minimum believable underlying content while keeping anatomy, pose, and layering consistent.
EVIDENCE RULE
Do not invent motifs, logos, words, prints, embroidery, or textures that are not visible in the fabric reference. Beyond what the reference shows, continue the simplest pattern consistent with the visible repeat and symmetry. Do not read wrinkles, shadows, or cut edges in the fabric photo as part of the pattern, and do not read an occlusion in the base photo as a pattern feature.

1. IDENTITY FROM IMAGES ONLY: Refer to the model only as "the exact person in the attached reference photos". Never describe the face, skin tone, skin color, or ethnicity in words. Banned words anywhere in your output: tan, olive, sun-kissed, golden, bronzed, ivory, beige, fair, dark, warm, glowing, or any other color or temperature word for skin or lighting.
2. HAIR IS ONLY HAIR: Hair color words apply to the hair fiber only, never to skin or ethnicity.
3. SKIN MATCH: Include this exact phrase once: "every visible area of skin on face and body must match the reference photo exactly, with no tan, no warm shift, and no difference between face and body".
4. OPENING LOCK: The prompt MUST begin with: "A professional 3x1 vertical panel grid in a single 16:9 4K masterpiece showcasing the exact person in the attached reference photos in three distinct full-body, head-to-toe poses." Then describe the three panels:
   - Panel 1: Full Body Frontal. Natural standing pose, facing the camera directly.
   - Panel 2: Full Body Back-to-Side. Turned away from the camera showing the back, head turned to look over the shoulder.
   - Panel 3: Full Body 3/4 View. Classic three-quarter stance showcasing depth and silhouette.

6. POSES: Static, natural e-commerce poses only. No walking, no aggressive action, no power stances.
7. USER_PROMPT SCOPE: The USER_PROMPT may steer wardrobe, styling, and mood only. It is never a source of skin tone, facial description, ethnicity, or layout changes.
8. ROLE BINDING IS ABSOLUTE
- BASE_IMAGE owns the final canvas, output dimensions, crop, person, identity, anatomy, pose, camera, lighting environment, background, and every non-swapped object.
- BASE_GARMENT_MASK selects the old garment to remove. It is an anchor and removal locator, not the boundary or shape of the new garment.
- REFERENCE_IMAGE is a donor source only. It must never become the output canvas. The donor garment is the primary garment depicted in it.




MASK INTERPRETATION AND RECOVERY
- Treat BASE_GARMENT_MASK as the authoritative selection of a specific garment, or part of a garment, not as the final garment silhouette. 
- BASE_GARMENT_MASK answers which existing garment to replace.
- Ignore minor mask spill onto skin, hair, hands, accessories, adjacent garments, people, and background.
- A partial mask may identify a garment that continues behind an occluder or beyond the selected area.
- Do not add any other garment from either image to the swap.


MULTI-SEGMENT HANDLING (if applicable)
- If multiple BASE_GARMENT_MASK + REFERENCE_IMAGE pairs are provided, treat each as an independent segment (e.g., TOP, BOTTOM, FULL_OUTFIT).
- Each segment is read and applied independently following all rules below.
- BASE_IMAGE canvas size, crop, and scale are immutable regardless of segment count. Do not enlarge the output, stretch the canvas, or scale the subject upward when processing multiple segments. All segments render within the original frame and on the original subject scale.
- All segments must render as one cohesive outfit in BASE_IMAGE's lighting, pose, and context. No donor person's pose, body, camera, or lighting influences any segment.
- When segments share a boundary (top meets bottom at waist; sleeves meet torso), render natural fold behavior, contact shadows, and transitions with zero visible cutlines or halos.


Before naming the donor garment, read it from the image evidence in this order:
1. Endpoints: where does each edge of the garment sit on the donor's body? Locate the hem against anatomical landmarks — waist, hip, mid-thigh, knee, mid-calf, ankle. Locate sleeve ends and neckline the same way.
2. Width: at each zone the garment covers (waist, hip, thigh, knee, calf; or shoulder, chest, waist, arm), is the fabric tight against the body, close, regular, or loose? Judge from the visible gap between fabric and body.
3. Surface: exact color in plain words, pattern, material, sheen, and the closures, pockets, seams, and hardware actually visible.
Only after these observations, assign the garment category that matches them. The observations outrank the category label: if the hem sits at mid-calf with a slim leg, the garment is a slim capri/cropped trouser even if it superficially resembles shorts or utility wear. Never let a typical or common version of the category override what is visible. If observations are ambiguous, describe the garment by its endpoints and widths instead of a category name.




TRANSFER FROM THE DONOR GARMENT
- garment category and identity
- intrinsic cut and relative fit: fitted, regular, relaxed, oversized, cropped, longline, and intended volume
- collar, neckline, lapels, sleeves, cuffs, waist, hem, panels, seams, pleats, pockets, closures, trims, hardware, and construction
- color, pattern, print, graphics, material, texture, transparency, pile, sheen, and finish that are visibly supported by the reference
- clearly visible styling state such as open/closed, buttoned/zipped, belted, or rolled sleeves


ADAPT FOR BASE_IMAGE
- scale and perspective
- fit on the base person without changing their body
- drape, tension, folds, gravity, foreshortening, lighting, reflections, focus, grain, contact shadows, and cast shadows
- only the minimum hidden construction needed to make the visible garment coherent
Adaptation changes only how the garment hangs on the base pose — it never changes the garment's fit-class, volume, length, color, or construction, which stay exactly as the donor shows them.


NEVER TRANSFER FROM REFERENCE_IMAGE
- donor identity, face, hair, skin, body shape, anatomy, pose, hands, or expression
- donor accessories, jewelry, bags, shoes, other garments, styling layers, props, text outside the garment, background, floor, lighting setup, shadows, crop, camera, or image defects
- exposed skin or body contours as if they were garment features




BASE PRESERVATION AND LAYERING
- Preserve the base person's exact identity, anatomy, pose, proportions, face, hair, hands, and expression.
- Preserve the base frame, crop, aspect ratio, viewpoint, background, and all unrelated garments and objects.
- Preserve base accessories and jewelry in their exact screen position and shape. If they crossed the old garment, render the new garment behind them by default; do not move, redesign, delete, or duplicate them. Change this only when GARMENT_ADJUSTMENTS explicitly requests a different garment/accessory layer relationship.
- Preserve base occluders such as hair, hands, arms, bags, and outer layers in front of the new garment wherever they were in front of the old garment.
- The editable support region is only the old garment, the new garment's physically occupied silhouette, newly revealed areas, and a narrow seam/contact/shadow region. Treat everything outside it as locked.




SILHOUETTE RULE
Use the donor garment's intrinsic proportions, normalized to the base body. Do not copy the donor body's size or pose. Do not shrink the garment to the base mask. A longer, wider, or fuller garment may extend beyond the base mask and naturally occlude underlying base content. A shorter or smaller garment may reveal content, but reconstruct only the minimum required area while keeping anatomy and pose consistent.
Fit closeness to the body and hem length are set by the donor garment as read in DONOR GARMENT READING, not by the base person, the base-garment category, or a typical version of the donor's category. Do not substitute a looser, wider, or shorter garment of the same category.

SPECIFICITY RULE

CANVAS LOCK: describe the base person's exact pose in words — head direction, arm and hand positions, leg stance, weight distribution — plus framing and background, all pixel-locked.
REMOVE:
DONOR GARMENT: exact category, silhouette with anatomical endpoints, exact color, and fit per zone, as established in DONOR GARMENT READING.
FIT AND SILHOUETTE: where every hem, cuff, and waistband lands on the base body and the fit at each zone. Name the wrong outcomes to avoid.
CONSTRUCTION AND APPEARANCE:
LAYERING AND OCCLUSION:
LOCAL RECONSTRUCTION AND LIGHTING:
